title: Video understanding
summary: Video is frames plus audio plus time. Managed analyzers sample about one frame per second at low resolution and transcribe speech, so fast events and fine on-screen text need your own sampling.
useIf: You need searchable scenes, summaries or fields from recorded video, and speech plus coarse visuals carry most of the meaning.
avoidIf: The answer depends on fast motion or tiny on-screen text, unless you control the frame sampling yourself.

explain.md: A vision model reads images, so video understanding is a sampling problem: which frames, at what resolution, plus the soundtrack. Azure Content Understanding's video analyzer takes about **1 frame per second**, resizes frames to **512 x 512 px**, and transcribes **speech only**, not music or ambient sound. It offers key frames, shot detection (`cameraShotTimesMs`) and custom segmentation (`enableSegment`), and segmentation spends generative model tokens even when no fields are defined [[r11]].

Versions matter. The GA API `2025-11-01` is the production choice. `2026-06-01-preview` adds agentic mode, in-page segmentation, signature detection and document metadata, and carries no SLA [[r10]] (checked 2026-10-13). If you sample frames yourself, cost is arithmetic: frames x tokens per frame, where tokens per frame follow the image rules in [[r1]].

explain.title: From clip to answer
explain.alt: A video splits into key frames and a speech transcript, which combine into timed segments and then fields or an index.

explain.title: Self-sampled frame cost
explain.expr: tokens = seconds x fps x tokens_per_frame

vars.v: gpt-4.1 `low` 85, `high` 255 at 512 x 512, patch model 308 (256 patches x 1.2, rounded up)

explain.example: A 10-minute clip at 1 fps is 600 frames: **51,000** tokens at `low` on gpt-4.1, **153,000** at `high`, and **184,800** on a patch model with multiplier 1.2. These are derived from [[r1]], not printed there.

explain.title: 512 x 512 loses fine text
explain.md: At the analyzer's frame size, small interface text and slide fine print are unreadable. Extract higher-resolution frames yourself and send them at `original` detail where supported (inference from the documented limits).

whereToUse: Media libraries that need scene segments, tags and descriptions
Training and meeting recordings with speech as the main carrier
Compliance review of recorded customer sessions
Short clips where every second matters and you sample frames yourself

use: The managed analyzer when speech and coarse scenes carry the meaning and you want key frames and shots
Your own sampling when you need higher resolution, a different rate or event-driven frames
Transcript only when the video is talking heads
avoid: 1 fps sampling for fast events such as impacts or quick gestures
Preview API versions in production, since they have no SLA
Segmentation turned on everywhere without a use for the segments
flips: Slides or screen recordings: add self-extracted frames at slide changes
Fast events: sample faster around triggers rather than for the whole clip
Cost spikes after enabling segmentation: restrict `enableSegment` to where it is used

pitfalls.symptom: Questions about on-screen numbers return nonsense
pitfalls.cause: Frames were resized to 512 x 512 and small text became unreadable
pitfalls.fix: Extract higher-resolution frames at slide changes and read them at `original` detail.

pitfalls.symptom: A quick event is never found
pitfalls.cause: Sampling at about 1 frame per second skips it
pitfalls.fix: Raise the rate around the event window or use a trigger-based sampler.

pitfalls.symptom: Output shape changes after a service update
pitfalls.cause: Production calls `2026-06-01-preview`, which has no SLA
pitfalls.fix: Pin the GA version `2025-11-01` and test previews elsewhere.

pitfalls.cause: Segmentation spends generative model tokens even with no fields
pitfalls.fix: Enable `enableSegment` only where the segments are consumed.

scenarios.title: Lectures with slides
scenarios.situation: A university indexes 3,000 hours of lectures. Slides carry formulas and small labels, and students ask what a slide said at minute 40.
constraints: Search must point to a time
scenarios.question: How do you index it?

options.name: Transcript for all, plus higher-resolution frames extracted at slide changes and read at `original` detail
options.why: Speech gives timestamps cheaply, and your own frames avoid the 512 x 512 limit [[r11]].
options.tradeoff: You build slide-change detection and own the frame pipeline.

options.name: Managed analyzer with default sampling
options.why: Gives key frames, shots and a transcript in one managed call.
options.tradeoff: Small slide text is lost at 512 x 512.

options.name: Caption a frame every second
options.why: Thousands of mostly redundant captions per lecture, with fine text still unreadable.

flips.then: Index the decks directly and align them to the transcript.

scenarios.takeaway: Index speech first and spend pixels on the slides.

scenarios.title: Fast events on a factory line
scenarios.situation: Short clips of a packing line must flag the moment an item drops. Drops last a fraction of a second. Volume is modest.
unknowns: Can a trigger (motion sensor) mark the window?
What frame rate do cameras record?
scenarios.question: How do you sample?

options.name: Sample densely around trigger windows with your own pipeline and a vision model
options.why: About 1 fps cannot see sub-second events, so rate must follow the event.
options.tradeoff: Token cost rises in the dense windows and you need a trigger.

options.name: Managed analyzer at default sampling
options.why: It samples about one frame per second and can step over the event.
options.tradeoff: Good for scene-level summaries of the same line.

options.name: Dense sampling of every clip at full rate
options.tradeoff: At 30 fps a 10-minute clip is 18,000 frames, which is expensive.

flips.then: Run a cheap motion filter first to select windows.

flips.if: Only an end-of-shift summary is needed

scenarios.takeaway: Sampling rate must match event duration.

quiz.q: You sample a 5-minute clip at 1 fps with 512 x 512 frames on a patch model with multiplier 1.2 (32 px patches). How many image tokens in total?
quiz.explain: 300 frames. Each frame is 256 patches x 1.2 = 307.2, rounded up to 308. 300 x 308 = 92,400.

quiz.q: Which statements match the documented behaviour of the Content Understanding video analyzer?
options: Segmentation can spend generative model tokens even with no fields
quiz.explain: The analyzer transcribes speech only, so the third statement is false. The other three are documented.

quiz.q: Which change most justifies building your own frame sampler?
options: On-screen text is small and must be read
The video is a talking head
quiz.explain: Small text is lost at the analyzer's 512 x 512 frames. Scene tags, talking heads and transcripts are what the managed analyzer already handles.

flashcards.front: What does the Content Understanding video analyzer sample and transcribe?
flashcards.back: About 1 frame per second, resized to 512 x 512 px, and speech only (no music or ambient sound). It adds key frames, shot detection and optional segmentation.

flashcards.front: Which Content Understanding API version should production use?
flashcards.back: GA `2025-11-01`. `2026-06-01-preview` has no SLA and adds agentic mode, in-page segmentation and signature detection.

flashcards.front: How do you estimate self-sampled video cost?
flashcards.back: Seconds x fps x tokens per frame, with tokens per frame from the model's image rules, for example 308 for a 512 x 512 frame on a 1.2 multiplier patch model.
